newsitem.title: UK: Royal Dutch/Shell posts 7 percent decline in profits.
newsitem.headline: Royal Dutch/Shell posts 7 percent decline in profits.

text.p: Royal Dutch/Shell Group said Thursday its profits declined 7 percent despite strong crude oil prices because of persistently low refining margins and a poor chemicals market.

The Anglo-Dutch oil giant said its profits, excluding an exceptional gain of 84 million pounds ($137 million) after a divestment in South Africa, fell to 1.117 billion pounds ($1.82 billion) in the third quarter, slightly lower than most analysts' forecasts.
That compared with 1.202 billion pounds ($1.95 billion) a year earlir.
Overall, it said, refining earnings fell 27 percent in the third quarter.

Nick Antill, an analyst at BZW, said the weak earnings appeared to be a result of an unusually high exploration write-off of 211 million pounds ($344 million), up from 131 million ($213 million) a year ago.
"It is a mere random event and has nothing to do with what actually happened in the quarter," Antill said.
In the chemicals sector, the group's earnings dropped 40 percent as prices still showed no firm sign of recovering from the slump that started about a year ago.

Oil prices, which have surged to their highest levels since the 1991 Gulf War, will remain volatile, while the chemicals sector shows improvements in only limited parts of the business, Royal Dutch/Shell Group said.
"Along with the industry, change can only come when there is significant growth in the industrial economies," the company, one of the world's biggest, said in a statement.
Royal Dutch Petroleum owns 60 percent of the group, and the remainder is held by Britain's Shell Transport and Trading.
The company said a rise of about $4.75 in the average oil price per barrel boosted production and exploration results. Increased crude production and gas sales outside the U.S. also helped.
But the higher oil price also meant higher costs for the refining operations and offset a surge in European middle distillate prices, Royal Dutch/Shell Group said.
Margins in the Asia-Pacific region were significantly weaker than in the second quarter, but slightly higher than in the same period last year.
In the United States, where Shell and Texaco Inc. plan to escape industry-wide overcapacity through a massive merger of their marketing and refining operations, maintenance shutdowns hurt results.
Analyst Irene Himona at SocGen said "Overall, there were no great surprises. It's just slightly disappointing."
